svg.text: Five questions that make antibiotic use rational
Resistance is not created in laboratories. It is created one unnecessary prescription at a time.
1. Does this patient have a bacterial infection at all?
Most fevers, coughs and sore throats are viral. An antibiotic changes nothing except the patient's flora.
2. Have specimens been taken before the first dose?
After the first dose the culture may grow nothing, and you lose the chance to narrow the treatment.
3. Is this the narrowest drug that will work?
Broad cover is for when you do not yet know. Once you know, narrow it. Broader is not stronger.
4. Can it go from the drip to the mouth yet?
A patient who is eating, afebrile and improving usually no longer needs the cannula that is infecting her.
5. When does it stop?
A stop or review date written at the start prevents the course that quietly runs for three weeks.
What patients in Ghana actually do
Buy a few capsules from a chemical seller,
take them until they feel better, and keep
the rest for next time or for a relative.
Ask without blame, or you will not be told.
Drugs that need blood levels checked
Some drugs have so narrow a margin that the
dose is set by measuring the level, not by
the patient's weight alone. The timing of the
sample matters as much as the result.
